The idea that wild animals are annoyances or threats that need to be eliminated is common in many parts of the world. However, often, unintended consequences occur because of this attitude. A balanced approach is needed, particularly between human safety and the well-being of the animals, which can be found when we grasp a proper understanding of their behavior as well as their role in their natural habitat. After all, we should acknowledge the fact that both humans and animals are temporary tenants of this precious planet. Neither is less valuable nor more valuable than the other. Throughout history, humans and animals have worked together in a variety of ways. Dogs helped round up sheep, horses and cows helped with farming, and some animals assisted with hunting and guarding. Raising and breeding animals has always been a vital part of human history. Recent studies, however, reveal there’s another aspect to this story. It turns out that wild animals, those that haven’t been specifically bred to live with humans, are also willing to form mutual relationships with humans. One outstanding example is in Laguna, Brazil, where dolphins and fishers have teamed up to catch fish for over 130 years. A 15-year study conducted by researchers used drones and underwater cameras to observe this unique partnership. When migrating mullets approach the shore in large groups, some dolphins drive them towards the coast, where fishers stand ready to catch them with their nets. The fishers watch the dolphins, looking for them to communicate that they will be making a “deep dive,” which lasts about 15 seconds. Fishers then cast their nets just as the dolphins drive the mullets towards the surface. As a result, the fishers catch much more fish, and the dolphins get to eat mullets trying to escape from the net. Amazingly, dolphins that engage in this fishing are more likely to live longer, by 13 percent. Without this cooperation, dolphins may end up swimming to areas where there aren’t many fish, and in doing so, get caught in illegal fishing nests. The 130-year partnership between the dolphins and the fishers of Laguna is more than just a way to catch fish. It’s a win-win for both humans and animals, a reminder of how our interactions and relationships with the natural world can be mutually beneficial. This harmony has kept the tradition alive for generations, and it continues to inspire us today.
answer: Balanced Humans Wild Animals

In short, BMR and TEF are the minimum energy required for the body (C)[stays / to stay] alive. The remaining 400 calories, or 20%, is used for things people choose to do, including various physical activities (PA) like working, playing, and moving around.
